slides.text: Every value in Go has a type, and Go checks it before the program runs. Here you use whole numbers, decimals, text and bools, convert between them by hand, and read the errors Go reports when types do not fit. The snippet is a map of the types, not Go.
slides.code:
whole numbers  int, int8, int64, uint8
decimals       float64
text           string
true or false  bool

exercises.title: Whole numbers
exercises.guide: Declare two whole numbers of different types and print them.

chunks.guide: `int` is the usual type for whole numbers.
Other types have a fixed size and range. `uint8` holds 0 to 255: the `u` means unsigned, so no negatives.

notes.text: A small number that is never negative.

exercises.title: Fit the number
exercises.guide: Pick a type that can hold 200.

exercises.title: Decimal numbers
exercises.guide: Declare two decimal numbers and print them.

chunks.guide: A number with a decimal point is a `float64`, the usual type for decimals.
A whole number also fits a `float64`: it is a decimal with nothing after the point.
A decimal that is whole prints without the point.

exercises.title: Why does it not compile?
exercises.guide: Read the message, then pick the cause.
exercises.code:
./main.go:8:14: invalid operation:
  count + price (mismatched types
  int and float64)
options: An int and a float64 cannot be added directly
exercises.explanation: Go never mixes number types on its own. Convert one side so both have the same type.

exercises.title: Convert a number
exercises.guide: Turn an `int` into a `float64`, and a `float64` into an `int`.

chunks.guide: A type used like a function converts the value. `count` itself stays an `int`.

notes.text: Makes a decimal copy of the value.

chunks.guide: Going back to `int` cuts off the decimals. It does not round.

exercises.title: What does it print?
exercises.guide: Read the code, then pick the output.
exercises.explanation: `uint8` holds 0 to 255. `big` is a variable, so Go does not stop it: 300 wraps around to 300 - 256 = 44.

exercises.title: Text and bools
exercises.guide: Declare a string and a bool, and ask the string for its length.

chunks.guide: Text is a `string`, written between double quotes.
`len` gives the length of a string, counted in bytes. Each of these letters is one byte.

notes.text: Built into Go, so it needs no import.

chunks.guide: A `bool` is `true` or `false`, and nothing else.

exercises.title: What does it print?
exercises.guide: Read the code, then pick the output.
exercises.explanation: `len` counts bytes, not letters. The letter `é` takes two bytes, so the five letters make 6 bytes.

exercises.title: A single character
exercises.guide: Store one character and print it in two ways.

chunks.guide: Single quotes make a **rune**: one character, kept as its Unicode number.
A rune prints as its number. `G` is 71.
Converting the rune to a `string` gives the character back as text.

exercises.title: A true or false value
exercises.guide: Go never turns a number into a bool. Give `open` a bool value.
